deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (from the previous page). This is Hilbert's attempt to prove the claim he states at the end of his 13th Paris problem (1900): there exist analytic functions of three variables that cannot be built by finitely many compositions of functions of two variables. He restricts to a chain-type composition. Unknown auxiliary functions x1,y1 of (x,y,z) satisfy a system (1), not visible here. x2=x2(x1,y1) and y2=y2(x1,y1) give the two PDEs (2). x3=x3(x2,y2) and y3=y3(x2,y2) give the two PDEs (3). In (3), the 3x3 determinant with columns grad x3 (or grad y3), grad x2, grad y2 vanishes. The general principle, stated on the previous page: w=W(u,v) with u,v functions of (x,y,z) holds iff grad w lies in span(grad u, grad v), i.e. det[grad w, grad u, grad v]=0.

THIS PAGE, part 1.
(a) The last step is f=F(x3,y3). By the same principle this gives (4): det[[f_x, (x3)_x, (y3)_x], [f_y, (x3)_y, (y3)_y], [f_z, (x3)_z, (y3)_z]] = 0.
(b) Count: (1)-(4) form 7 PDEs (2+2+2+1, assuming (1) has two equations). The unknowns are f, x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3.
(c) Non-degeneracy condition: not all 2x2 minors of the matrix [grad x_k, grad y_k] (first column omitted) may vanish identically in (2),(3),(4). Otherwise x_k and y_k are functionally dependent, the determinant vanishes for every f, and the system imposes no condition.
(d) Goal: eliminating x1,...,y3 should give a genuine 'Endgleichung' F_n(f)=0. This is a nontrivial (presumably algebraic) partial differential equation of finite order satisfied by every f obtainable through n compositions.
(e) Two ways to prove nontriviality are mentioned. One is counting Taylor coefficients, 'as in my earlier proofs'. The other is a general criterion for when a PDE system is 'wirklich bestimmt' (really determined). Hilbert flags that criterion as a desideratum, not as something he has.
(f) Existence argument: for each n there is a nontrivial PDE F_n(f)=0. Choose an everywhere-convergent (entire) power series P(x,y,z) satisfying none of the countably many equations F_1=0, F_2=0, ... Then P is a function of the required kind. [My fill: such a P exists because each F_n(f)=0 is a closed, nowhere-dense condition on the Taylor coefficients. A Baire-category argument, or a diagonal choice of coefficients, avoids all of them while keeping the series entire.]

THIS PAGE, part 2 (new topic). A plan for a new proof of 'my independence theorem' (Hilbert's invariant integral / Unabhängigkeitssatz, 1900).
(a) Setting: a problem of Mayer/Monge type. Curves (y(x),z(x)) are subject to the differential constraint f(y',z',y,z,x)=0. They start at the fixed point (a1,b1,c1) and end at x=a2, y=b2, with z(a2) to be minimised.
(b) Regard the minimum Z as a function of the endpoint (a2,b2), i.e. the value function z=z(x,y). Derive its first-order PDE in two steps: differentiate along the extremal, then in the transversal direction at the endpoint.
(c) Transversality comes (continued next page) from the boundary term of the first variation, after integration by parts, set to zero. Modern reading: deriving the Hamilton-Jacobi equation for the value function of a Mayer problem. The invariance of the Hilbert integral then follows from it.
(d) Example of mine: z'=sqrt(1+y'^2) gives Z=c1+sqrt((x-a1)^2+(y-b1)^2), which satisfies Z_x^2+Z_y^2=1.
errors: (4) as transcribed reads (f_x)_x, (f_y)_y, (f_z)_z. The intended entries are f_x, f_y, f_z (first derivatives of f). This is a notational slip, either Hilbert's or the transcriber's.

The chain model x1,y1 -> x2,y2 -> x3,y3 -> f is a special case. A general finite superposition is a tree that may reuse x,y,z at each level. Hilbert's restriction to this chain form is not justified on this page.

The 7 equations are matched against 7 unknown functions, so naive counting does not show that elimination gives a nontrivial condition on f. Hilbert himself flags this gap: he says one needs a criterion for a 'really determined' system, or the coefficient count.
Choosing an entire P that avoids all F_n=0 requires each F_n to be a genuine (e.g. algebraic, finite-order) differential relation. Hilbert does not establish this here.
Part 2 is only a plan. The transversality computation and the derivation of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation are deferred to the next page and not executed.

results.what: f=F(u,v) iff det[grad f, grad u, grad v]=0 (given grad u, grad v independent), used to encode compositions as PDEs

Strategy: each n-fold superposition of two-variable functions satisfies a nontrivial PDE F_n(f)=0; an entire function avoiding all countably many F_n gives an analytic f(x,y,z) that is not such a superposition
results.modern_name: Differential-algebraic / coefficient-counting proof of the analytic case of Hilbert's 13th problem
results.usually_credited_to: Claimed without proof by Hilbert (1900, 13th problem); related differential-algebraic arguments by Ostrowski (1920); smooth-class results by Vitushkin (1954)

results.what: Plan to prove the independence theorem for a Mayer-type problem with constraint f(y',z',y,z,x)=0 via the PDE for the minimal value as a function of the endpoint, with transversality from the boundary term
results.modern_name: Value function / Hamilton-Jacobi equation for a Mayer problem; Hilbert invariant integral
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (1900; Math. Ann. 1906 for Lagrange problems); Hamilton-Jacobi; Carathéodory's field approach

deep.surprise_reason: It is already known that Hilbert claimed the analytic non-superposition result in 1900, citing a 'rigorous argument'. This page shows a concrete form of that argument: PDE elimination via Jacobian determinants, plus an entire function avoiding countably many PDEs. It also shows his awareness that the nontriviality step needed a criterion he lacked. That is a notable unpublished detail, but not a new result. The variational part is a routine restatement of a known topic.

checkable.sympy: x,y,z=symbols('x y z'); X=Function('X')(x,y,z); Y=Function('Y')(x,y,z); F=Function('F'); f=F(X,Y); simplify(Matrix([[diff(f,v),diff(X,v),diff(Y,v)] for v in (x,y,z)]).det())
checkable.asserts: Equation (4): for f=F(X,Y) the Jacobian determinant is identically 0.

checkable.sympy: x,y,z=symbols('x y z'); X=Function('X')(x,y,z); g=Function('g'); Y=g(X); f=Function('f')(x,y,z); simplify(Matrix([[diff(f,v),diff(X,v),diff(Y,v)] for v in (x,y,z)]).det())
checkable.asserts: If the 2x2 minors of [grad X, grad Y] vanish (Y a function of X), the determinant vanishes for arbitrary f. This is why Hilbert requires non-vanishing minors.

checkable.sympy: x,y,a,b,c=symbols('x y a b c',real=True); Z=c+sqrt((x-a)**2+(y-b)**2); simplify(diff(Z,x)**2+diff(Z,y)**2-1)
checkable.asserts: Example Mayer problem z'=sqrt(1+y'^2) with fixed start: the minimal z as a function of the endpoint satisfies the Hamilton-Jacobi (eikonal) equation Z_x^2+Z_y^2=1 (result 0).

transcription_corrections: In (4) the first column is most likely f_x, f_y, f_z (or (f)_x, (f)_y, (f)_z), not (f_x)_x, (f_y)_y, (f_z)_z.
'{+bestimme+} [-sätze-]': the deleted word is more plausibly 'setze'; the inserted 'bestimme' is written above the line.
'f ist eine gesuchte Funktion' refers to the series P just constructed, i.e. P is a sought function.
In the variational part, the deleted symbol before 'y = b_2' is a crossed-out letter; the reading 'x=a_2, y=b_2' is correct.
